title: Hugging Face Transformers
summary: Hugging Face is the GitHub of machine learning models. Its Transformers library lets you download and run thousands of pretrained models in a few lines of code. This is the single most important practical tool for a working GenAI engineer.
content:
# Hugging Face Transformers ##### Six weeks of work, replaced by three lines In early 2019, a startup in Pune quoted a client six weeks to build a sentiment classifier for Marathi and English product reviews. The estimate was honest: collect and label data, build a tokenizer, train an LSTM, tune it, wrap it in an API. Two engineers, six weeks. They delivered in nine days. Not because they worked faster, but because someone found `huggingface/transformers` on GitHub and realised the model already existed. ```python from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis") print(classifier("The delivery was late but the product is excellent.")) # [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.9891}] ``` Three lines. A 66-million-parameter transformer, downloaded, loaded, and running. This is the practical reality of GenAI engineering in 2026: **you almost never train from scratch.** Somebody has already trained a model close to what you need, published the weights, and documented how to use them. Your job is to find it, evaluate it, adapt it, and ship it. Hugging Face is where that happens. Over a million public models, 250,000 datasets, and one consistent API across all of them. Wolf et al.'s 2020 paper describing the library is now among the most-cited software papers in NLP — not for algorithmic novelty, but because standardising access to models mattered enormously. ##### The Hub The Hugging Face Hub is Git for models. Every model is a repository containing weights, config, tokenizer files, and a README (the model card). Finding the right one is a real skill. The filters that matter: - **Task** — text-classification, summarization, question-answering, text-generation, feature-extraction. - **Language** — filter to `hi`, `ta`, `bn`, `mr` for Indian languages. - **Library** — PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX. - **Sort by downloads** — a proxy for reliability. A model with 4 million monthly downloads has been battle-tested; one with 40 has not. - **License** — critical and routinely ignored. Apache-2.0 and MIT are commercially safe. Llama's license has usage restrictions. Some models are research-only, and shipping one in a paid product is a real legal problem. Model naming follows `organisation/model-name`: ``` distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── fine-tuned on SST-2 sentiment │ │ └── lowercases input │ └── base size (not large/small) └── distilled BERT ``` Reading that name tells you the architecture, size, casing behaviour, and training task before you download anything. ##### Pipelines The `pipeline` API bundles tokenizer, model, and post-processing into one callable. It is the fastest path from idea to working code. ```python from transformers import pipeline # Sentiment sentiment = pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english") print(sentiment(["Loved the biryani.", "Cold food, rude staff."])) # Summarization summarizer = pipeline("summarization", model="facebook/bart-large-cnn") article = """...""" # a long news article print(summarizer(article, max_length=90, min_length=30, do_sample=False)) # Question answering (extractive — pulls a span from the context) qa = pipeline("question-answering", model="distilbert-base-cased-distilled-squad") print(qa(question="What is the notice period?", context="Either party may terminate with 60 days written notice.")) # {'answer': '60 days', 'score': 0.87, 'start': 42, 'end': 49} # Zero-shot classification — labels you invent at runtime, no training zs = pipeline("zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli") print(zs("My UPI payment failed but money was debited.", candidate_labels=["billing", "technical", "delivery", "account"])) # Named entity recognition ner = pipeline("ner", model="dslim/bert-base-NER", aggregation_strategy="simple") print(ner("Priya Sharma joined Infosys in Bengaluru last March.")) # Text generation gen = pipeline("text-generation", model="gpt2") print(gen("The future of AI in India", max_new_tokens=50, do_sample=True, temperature=0.8, truncation=True)) # Embeddings (feature extraction) embed = pipeline("feature-extraction", model="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") ``` **Zero-shot classification deserves attention.** You define the labels at call time — no training data, no fine-tuning. It works by reframing classification as natural language inference ("Does this text entail the label 'billing'?"). Accuracy is lower than a fine-tuned model, but for prototyping or for a long tail of rare categories it is remarkable. **Performance settings you should always set in production:** ```python import torch pipe = pipeline( "sentiment-analysis", model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english", device=0 if torch.cuda.is_available() else -1, # 0 = first GPU, -1 = CPU batch_size=32, # batch, don't loop torch_dtype=torch.float16, # half precision on GPU ) results = pipe(list_of_1000_texts) # batched internally — far faster than a loop ``` Passing a list rather than looping is often a 10× speedup, and it is the single most common performance mistake beginners make with pipelines. ##### AutoModel and AutoTokenizer Pipelines are convenient but opaque. When you need control — custom pooling, access to hidden states, fine-tuning — drop one level down. ```python import torch from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification CKPT = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(CKPT) model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(CKPT) model.eval() texts = ["The service was outstanding.", "Never ordering from here again."] # 1. Tokenize inputs = tokenizer(texts, padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=256, return_tensors="pt") print(inputs.keys()) # input_ids, attention_mask print(tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(inputs["input_ids"][0])) # 2. Forward pass with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model(**inputs) # 3. Post-process probs = torch.softmax(outputs.logits, dim=-1) for text, p in zip(texts, probs): label = model.config.id2label[p.argmax().item()] print(f"{label:9s} {p.max():.4f} {text}") ``` Those three steps are exactly what `pipeline` does internally. Once you have seen them, pipelines stop being magic. **The `Auto` classes** inspect the checkpoint's config and instantiate the right architecture. `AutoModel` for BERT gives you `BertModel`; for GPT-2 it gives `GPT2Model`. This is what lets you swap models by changing one string. The task-specific heads: | Class | Output | Use for | |---|---|---| | `AutoModel` | Hidden states | Embeddings, custom heads | | `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` | Logits over classes | Sentiment, topic, intent | | `AutoModelForTokenClassification` | Logits per token | NER, POS tagging | | `AutoModelForQuestionAnswering` | Start/end span logits | Extractive QA | | `AutoModelForCausalLM` | Next-token logits | GPT-style generation | | `AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM` | Encoder-decoder output | Translation, summarisation | **One rule that prevents a whole class of bugs: always load the tokenizer and model from the same checkpoint.** A mismatched pair produces token IDs the model was never trained on, and you get plausible-looking garbage with no error message. ##### The Datasets library `datasets` handles loading, transforming, and streaming data — memory-mapped via Apache Arrow, so a 100 GB dataset does not need 100 GB of RAM. ```python from datasets import load_dataset, Dataset # From the Hub imdb = load_dataset("imdb") print(imdb) print(imdb["train"][0]["text"][:200], imdb["train"][0]["label"]) # From your own files local = load_dataset("csv", data_files={"train": "train.csv", "test": "test.csv"}) local = load_dataset("json", data_files="tickets.jsonl") # From a pandas DataFrame import pandas as pd ds = Dataset.from_pandas(pd.read_parquet("reviews.parquet")) # Transformations — batched map is much faster def tokenize(batch): return tokenizer(batch["text"], truncation=True, max_length=256) tokenized = imdb.map(tokenize, batched=True, num_proc=4, remove_columns=["text"]) # Filtering, shuffling, splitting long_only = imdb["train"].filter(lambda x: len(x["text"]) > 500) sample = imdb["train"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(2000)) splits = sample.train_test_split(test_size=0.2, seed=42) # Streaming — for datasets too large to download stream = load_dataset("c4", "en", split="train", streaming=True) for i, row in enumerate(stream): if i >= 3: break print(row["text"][:120]) ``` `batched=True` with `num_proc` is the difference between tokenizing 25,000 documents in eight seconds and eight minutes. ##### Model cards A model card is the README, and reading it is not optional. Before using any model in production, check: - **Intended use and limitations** — what it was built for, and explicitly what it was not. - **Training data** — domain, language, time period. A sentiment model trained on movie reviews may do poorly on medical complaints. - **Evaluation results** — on which benchmarks, and how do they compare? - **Bias and ethical considerations** — Day 42's concerns apply directly. - **License** — the commercial question. - **Model size and hardware requirements.** A concrete example of why: `bert-base-uncased` lowercases everything. If your task is NER on Indian names, casing is a strong signal and you want `bert-base-cased`. That is in the model card, in the name, and it will cost you two days if you skip both. ##### Choosing a model ```mermaid flowchart TD A["What is the task?"] --> B{"Understanding
or generation?"} B -->|Understanding| C["Encoder: BERT family"] B -->|Generation| D["Decoder: GPT/Llama family"] B -->|Transformation| E["Seq2seq: T5/BART"] C --> F{"Language?"} F -->|English| G["distilbert / roberta-base"] F -->|Indic| H["MuRIL / IndicBERT"] F -->|Multilingual| I["xlm-roberta-base"] D --> J{"Constraint?"} J -->|Speed & cost| K["Small open model,
1-7B, quantized"] J -->|Quality| L["API model or
large open model"] G --> M["Check: downloads,
license, model card"] H --> M I --> M K --> M L --> M ``` The practical heuristic: **start small.** DistilBERT before BERT-large, a 7B open model before a 70B one. Measure whether the small one is good enough for your actual task, because it is often within two points and costs a fraction to run. ##### Common mistakes - **Mismatched tokenizer and model checkpoint** — silent, confusing failures. - **Looping over texts one at a time** instead of passing a list for batching. - **Forgetting `device=0`**, running on CPU while a GPU sits idle. - **Forgetting `model.eval()` and `torch.no_grad()`** at inference. - **Not reading the license**, then discovering a research-only model is in your paid product. - **Ignoring `max_length`**, silently truncating long documents. - **Using an English model for Hindi or Tamil** instead of MuRIL/IndicBERT/XLM-R. - **`map()` without `batched=True`**, making preprocessing 50× slower. - **Downloading a 13 GB model to test an idea** when a 250 MB one would answer the question. - **Assuming the top search result is best** — sort by downloads and read the card. - **Not pinning the `transformers` version**, so the API shifts under you. - **Sending private data to the Inference API** without checking data handling terms. ##### Hands-on: use three pipelines, then look inside Your practical task is the pipeline API for sentiment, summarization, and generation with different models. Do sentiment twice — once with the default model and once with `cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest` — on the same inputs, especially inputs with sarcasm or mixed sentiment. The disagreements are informative: they show you that "sentiment analysis" is not one task but a family of them, and model choice encodes assumptions about your domain. The mini project is a multi-task Streamlit app with sentiment, summarization, and QA. Two engineering details matter here. Cache the models with `@st.cache_resource` so they load once rather than on every interaction — without it your app reloads 500 MB per click. And show the confidence score alongside every prediction, not just the label, so users can see when the model is unsure. That is a small UX decision with real trust implications. The assignment benchmarks three models on one task for speed and quality. Build a small table: model name, parameters, disk size, inference time for 100 examples, and accuracy on a held-out set you label yourself. The pattern you will usually find — that a distilled model is 3× faster for 1–2 points less accuracy — is exactly the trade-off you will be asked to reason about in interviews and in production planning. ##### Key takeaways - **You almost never train from scratch.** Finding, evaluating, and adapting an existing model is the core practical skill of GenAI engineering. - **`pipeline` is three lines from idea to working code**; `AutoTokenizer` + `AutoModel` is the level below when you need control, and it does exactly what the pipeline does. - **Always pair tokenizer and model from the same checkpoint**, and always batch by passing a list rather than looping. - **Read the model card before you commit** — intended use, training data, bias, and especially the license. - **Start small and measure.** DistilBERT often gets within two points of BERT-large at a third of the cost, and knowing that number is more valuable than assuming.
